title: AI Ethics & Safety
overview: Building AI that works is hard. Building AI that works and is safe, fair, and trustworthy is harder. This lecture covers the real risks that come with deploying AI systems at scale — algorithmic bias, hallucinations, deepfakes, and the principles of responsible AI development.

data.body: AI systems are only as fair as the data they are trained on — and the data reflects a world that has never been fair. Algorithmic bias is not a bug. It is the model accurately learning the biases encoded in historical human decisions.

A biased AI system produces systematically unfair outcomes for certain groups — often based on race, gender, age, or socioeconomic status. The model is doing exactly what it learned from historical data. The data was biased; the model learned the bias.

Training data bias: the dataset over-represents certain groups. Label bias: human annotators encode cultural assumptions. Sampling bias: data collected from non-representative populations. Feedback loops: biased predictions create biased new data.

A system can be discriminatory even without any protected characteristic as an explicit input. If zip code is a proxy for race, predicting from zip code can produce racially biased outcomes — and removing race from the input does not fix this.

Demographic parity: equal positive prediction rates across groups. Equalised odds: equal true positive and false positive rates. Calibration: predicted probabilities match actual rates for all groups. These metrics often cannot all be satisfied simultaneously.

data.text: You cannot simply remove protected attributes to make a model fair. If the data reflects historical injustice, the model will learn to perpetuate it through proxy variables.

blocks.title: Bias Hides in Training Data Like Contraband Hides in Luggage
blocks.subtitle: Security can miss dangerous items if the scanner was only trained to detect certain shapes. AI misses fairness problems if the training data only reflected certain populations.

panels.label: Real World
panels.description: If airport scanners were trained only on bags from travellers from one country, they might be less accurate for bags packed differently. The tool becomes biased by the unrepresentative training sample.

panels.label: The Pattern
panels.description: A tool trained on biased data learns to work well for the majority it saw — and poorly for the groups it didn't. The bias is invisible from inside the system; it only appears when you test across diverse groups.

visual.conclusion: Bias must be measured and addressed

panels.label: AI
panels.description: Criminal risk scoring tools, credit algorithms, medical diagnostic models, and hiring filters have all been found to produce disparate outcomes for racial, gender, or economic groups — not through intentional discrimination, but through biased training data.

blocks.insight: Algorithmic bias is automation of historical inequality. Deploying AI without fairness audits at scale makes discrimination faster, not smaller.
blocks.reinforcement: Biased data → biased model. The algorithm didn't choose to discriminate — it learned to from historical patterns.

data.body: Algorithmic bias is not theoretical. The COMPAS recidivism algorithm, widely used in US courts, was found to falsely label Black defendants as high-risk for re-offending at nearly twice the rate of white defendants — while simultaneously underestimating risk for white defendants. Amazon's hiring tool penalised resumes containing the word women's because it was trained on a decade of predominantly male hiring data. These are not failures of technology — they are failures of the data that shaped it.

data.text: The COMPAS algorithm was no less accurate for Black defendants overall — it was equally accurate but exhibited equalised odds violation. A model can be equally accurate across groups while systematically treating one group unfairly. Accuracy is not fairness.
Try It Yourself: Identify the Source of Bias

challenges.title: Spot the Source
challenges.objective: Identify which source of bias is at play in each scenario
challenges.instruction: Read each scenario and tap the correct bias source from the choices below.

apps.name: A facial recognition system fails to accurately identify people with darker skin tones because the training dataset contained 80% lighter-skinned faces.
apps.explanation: The training data was collected from a non-representative population. The model never learned to handle diverse skin tones.

apps.name: A resume screening tool is trained on resumes of past successful hires — almost all men — and learns to penalise candidates who attended women's colleges.
apps.explanation: The historical hiring data reflected past human bias. The model simply learned the pattern: past hires were mostly men.

apps.name: A loan approval model does not use race as an input, but it uses postal code, which strongly correlates with racial demographics in the training area.
apps.explanation: Removing the protected attribute (race) does not prevent the model from using a proxy (postal code) that correlates with it.

apps.name: A content moderation AI flags posts from minority-language speakers at higher rates because the human moderators who labelled the training data misunderstood cultural context.
apps.explanation: The human annotators introduced their own cultural assumptions when labelling, creating biased ground truth for the model to learn from.

apps.name: A predictive policing model sends more officers to high-crime neighbourhoods. More officers find more crime there. The model sees rising crime and sends even more officers — while low-crime areas remain under-policed.
apps.explanation: The model's predictions create new data that reinforces the original bias. More policing finds more crime, which justifies more policing.

challenges.explanation: Each scenario illustrates a different source of algorithmic bias. Sampling bias comes from unrepresentative data. Training data bias comes from historical patterns. Label bias comes from human annotator assumptions. Feedback loops are self-reinforcing cycles. Proxy discrimination uses correlated variables to stand in for protected attributes.

blocks.title: What Makes Algorithmic Bias Dangerous
blocks.body: Bias is dangerous because it operates at a scale and invisibility that human bias never could. A biased human affects dozens of people. A biased AI affects millions. And because the AI appears objective and mathematical, the bias is invisible to everyone — including its creators.
bullets: Scale amplifies harm — biased decisions affect millions instead of dozens
Bias is invisible from inside the system — standard accuracy metrics won't reveal it
Fairness metrics often conflict — demographic parity and equalised odds cannot always be satisfied simultaneously

data.code:
# Calculate key fairness metrics for a binary classifier
# Two groups: Group A and Group B

predictions = [
    {"group": "A", "actual": 1, "predicted": 1},
    {"group": "A", "actual": 1, "predicted": 1},
    {"group": "A", "actual": 0, "predicted": 0},
    {"group": "A", "actual": 1, "predicted": 0},
    {"group": "A", "actual": 0, "predicted": 1},
    {"group": "B", "actual": 1, "predicted": 0},
    {"group": "B", "actual": 0, "predicted": 1},
    {"group": "B", "actual": 1, "predicted": 1},
    {"group": "B", "actual": 1, "predicted": 0},
    {"group": "B", "actual": 0, "predicted": 0},
]

def fairness_metrics(data, group_label):
    g = [d for d in data if d["group"] == group_label]
    tp = sum(1 for d in g if d["actual"] == 1 and d["predicted"] == 1)
    fn = sum(1 for d in g if d["actual"] == 1 and d["predicted"] == 0)
    fp = sum(1 for d in g if d["actual"] == 0 and d["predicted"] == 1)
    tn = sum(1 for d in g if d["actual"] == 0 and d["predicted"] == 0)
    tpr = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0
    fpr = fp / (fp + tn) if (fp + tn) > 0 else 0
    return { "TPR": round(tpr, 3), "FPR": round(fpr, 3) }

for group in ["A", "B"]:
    m = fairness_metrics(predictions, group)
    print(f"Group {group}: TPR = {m['TPR']}, FPR = {m['FPR']}")

print("\nEqualised odds requires TPR and FPR to be equal across groups.")

data.body: Equalised odds — equal True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate across groups — is one of the most widely accepted fairness criteria. The code above shows how to compute it for two groups. If the rates differ significantly, the model does not satisfy equalised odds, even if its overall accuracy is high.

blocks.title: Detecting Bias in Training Data
blocks.instructions: Analyze training data to detect gender bias when data excludes certain groups.

# Detect bias in training data
applicants = [

male_scores = [a["score"] for a in applicants if a["gender"] == "M"]
avg = sum(male_scores) / len(male_scores)

print(f"Average male score: {avg}")
print(f"Alice ({applicants[0]['score']}) would be compared to male average: {avg}")
print("Issue: Female applicants excluded from training data!")

data.body: Modern AI systems can generate content that looks and sounds authoritative but is completely fabricated. AI hallucinations produce false facts with high confidence. Deepfakes produce synthetic media indistinguishable from real. Both undermine the foundations of shared reality.

Language models hallucinate when they generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information. They have no concept of truth — they generate whatever token is most probable given the context. Citations, names, and statistics can all be fabricated.

LLMs are trained to produce likely continuations, not true ones. When the model doesn't know something, it generates what seems most probable — which can look like a confident, detailed answer. The model has no internal fact-checker.

Generative models can create synthetic images, audio, and video of real people saying or doing things they never said or did. Deepfake technology is widely available. Detection is an ongoing arms race with generation.

Deepfake detection uses classifiers trained to spot generation artefacts — unnatural blinking patterns, inconsistent lighting, compression signatures from generative models. But as generators improve, detectors must constantly retrain.

data.text: A language model has no concept of truth. It only has a concept of likely. These two things are not the same.

blocks.title: AI Hallucinations Are Like a Broken GPS
blocks.subtitle: A GPS that confidently routes you into a lake isn't lying — it is following its model of the world, which no longer matches reality. Confident output is not the same as correct output.

panels.label: Real World
panels.description: GPS gives confident directions to a road that was built over a year ago and hasn't been updated in the maps. It isn't malfunctioning — it is confidently following a model that no longer matches reality.

panels.label: The Pattern
panels.description: Confidence and correctness are independent. A system can be highly confident and completely wrong. The absence of uncertainty signals is not evidence of truth — it is evidence that the system lacks uncertainty awareness.

panels.label: AI
panels.description: Language models produce the most probable continuation of text — not the most truthful one. When a model doesn't know something, it generates a confident-sounding answer because that is what training rewarded.

blocks.insight: Do not trust AI output on high-stakes factual questions without verification. Confidence is not correctness.
blocks.reinforcement: LLMs generate fluent text by predicting likely tokens — not by checking facts. Confidence ≠ correctness.

data.body: In 2023, a lawyer submitted a legal brief containing six fake court citations generated by ChatGPT. The attorney had asked the model to find precedents — and it invented them, complete with realistic-looking case numbers and judges' names. The model was not trying to deceive. It was doing exactly what it was trained to do: produce the most plausible continuation of the prompt. The difference between a hallucination and a fact is invisible to the model itself.

data.text: The cost of hallucination scales with deployment. A chatbot hallucinating a recipe causes a bad dinner. A medical chatbot hallucinating a drug interaction warning — or failing to warn — causes real harm. Always verify AI outputs in high-stakes domains.
Try It Yourself: Fact or Hallucination?

challenges.title: Spot the Hallucination
challenges.objective: Distinguish between verified facts and likely AI hallucinations
challenges.instruction: Read each AI-generated statement and decide whether it is a verified fact or a likely hallucination.

apps.name: "Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911 for her work on radioactivity."
apps.explanation: This is accurate. Marie Curie did win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911.

apps.name: "The population of Tokyo in 2025 was 37.4 million people, according to the Japan Statistical Yearbook."
apps.explanation: The specific citation is fabricated. While Tokyo's population is around 37 million, the model generated a citation that does not exist. This is a classic hallucination pattern.

apps.name: "The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889 as the entrance arch for the World's Fair."
apps.explanation: This is correct. The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 for the Exposition Universelle.

apps.name: "According to a 2023 study published in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, transformer models with more than 175 billion parameters show a 47% reduction in hallucination rate when fine-tuned on curated factual datasets."
apps.explanation: The citation sounds plausible but is fabricated. The specific study does not exist in that journal. LLMs often generate convincing but fake academic references.

apps.name: "Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure."
apps.explanation: This is a basic scientific fact that the model is very likely to have in its training data.

challenges.explanation: The pattern is clear: well-known facts are reliably generated. Specific citations, statistics, and obscure claims — especially those that look just plausible enough — are the most common hallucination type. Always verify claims that come with specific numbers or citations.

blocks.title: Why Hallucinations Are Hard to Fix
blocks.body: Hallucinations are not a bug — they are a feature of how LLMs work. The training objective is to predict the next token accurately, not to determine truth. A model that produces a plausible falsehood gets the same reward as one that produces a verified truth, as long as both are fluent.
bullets: The training objective is next-token prediction — truth is not part of the loss function
Deepfakes and detection are in an ongoing arms race — each new generator closes the gaps detectors rely on
Mitigation strategies like RAG, output verification, and human-in-the-loop review help but are not perfect solutions

data.code:
# Simple hallucination simulation: model knows some facts, fabricates others

known_facts = {
    "capital of France": "Paris",
    "first president of the US": "George Washington",
    "chemical symbol for gold": "Au",
    "speed of light (m/s)": "299,792,458",
}

def model_response(query):
    if query in known_facts:
        return known_facts[query], "high confidence"
    else:
        return f"According to recent research, {query} was first documented in 2019.", "high confidence"

queries = [
    "capital of France",
    "first president of the US",
    "population of Mars in 2026",
    "inventor of the quantum internet",
]

for q in queries:
    answer, confidence = model_response(q)
    status = "✅" if q in known_facts else "❌ HALLUCINATION"
    print(f"Q: {q}")
    print(f"A: {answer}  ({confidence})  {status}")
    print()

print("The model is equally confident for known facts and hallucinations.")

data.body: The critical issue is that confidence is not correlated with correctness. The model produces both true and false outputs with the same high confidence. This is why users cannot rely on the model's own certainty signals — and why external verification is essential in any safety-critical application.

blocks.hint: Hallucinations happen when AI confidently generates false information because it doesn't know the answer.

data.body: Responsible AI is not a checklist — it is a practice. It means building systems with safety and fairness as design goals from the start, not as patches applied after deployment. The technical choices made during development have social consequences at scale.

AI systems that make decisions affecting people should be explainable. Black-box models may be accurate, but when a loan is denied or a medical diagnosis is made, the affected person has a right to understand why.

When an AI system causes harm, someone must be accountable — the developer, the deployer, or both. Systems need audit trails, version control of models, and documented decision rationale so accountability can be assigned.

AI models trained on personal data can inadvertently memorise and reproduce it. Privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy, federated learning, and model auditing help ensure training data cannot be extracted from deployed models.

High-stakes AI decisions — medical, legal, financial, criminal justice — should have meaningful human oversight, not just human approval of whatever the model recommends. The human in the loop must have the information and authority to override.

data.text: At scale, AI systems shape what people see, what they are offered, who gets loans, who gets hired. Building responsibly is not optional — it is an ethical obligation.

blocks.title: Responsible AI Routes Decisions Like GPS Routes Around Hazards
blocks.subtitle: GPS avoids toll roads when you opt out, avoids flooded routes it knows are dangerous, and always shows you the route it chose and why. Responsible AI does the same: explain the path, allow override, avoid known harms.

panels.label: Real World
panels.description: A responsible GPS shows you its route and the alternatives. It warns you about road hazards. It lets you override its recommendation. And if a bridge is closed, it reroutes before you drive into the problem.

panels.label: The Pattern
panels.description: Transparency: show your reasoning. Accountability: log every decision. Safety: detect and avoid known failure modes. Human control: allow meaningful override at every step. These are design choices, not afterthoughts.

panels.label: AI
panels.description: Responsible AI embeds these principles at every stage: dataset curation, model training, deployment monitoring, and incident response. An AI system that causes harm without accountability is not a product — it is a risk.

blocks.insight: Responsible AI is not about making AI less powerful — it is about making powerful AI trustworthy.
blocks.reinforcement: Transparency, fairness, and human oversight aren't limitations — they're the infrastructure that makes AI trustworthy.

data.body: When an AI system makes a mistake, the consequences can ripple across millions of people before anyone notices. An automated hiring system can reject thousands of qualified candidates based on biased criteria. A content recommendation algorithm can radicalise users by optimising engagement over safety. A medical diagnostic tool can systematically misdiagnose certain populations. The common thread is not malicious intent — it is the absence of accountability infrastructure embedded in the system from the start.

data.text: The EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk level. High-risk systems (medical devices, hiring tools, credit scoring, law enforcement) must meet strict transparency, documentation, and human oversight requirements before deployment. Regulation is catching up.
Try It Yourself: Responsible AI Decisions

challenges.title: Responsible AI in Practice
challenges.objective: Match each scenario to the responsible AI principle at stake
challenges.instruction: Read each scenario and tap the correct responsible AI principle from the choices below.

apps.name: A hospital deploys an AI diagnostic system, but doctors cannot explain why it made certain predictions. Patients are not told how decisions about their health are being made.
apps.explanation: The system is operating as a black box. Patients and doctors have a right to understand the reasoning behind medical decisions.

apps.name: A self-driving car causes an accident. The company claims 'the model made a mistake' and no individual is responsible. The system logs were not retained.
apps.explanation: Without audit trails and clear responsibility assignment, no one is accountable when AI causes harm. This is a fundamental responsible AI failure.

apps.name: A language model trained on user conversations can reproduce verbatim sentences from specific users when prompted correctly, including personal information those users shared.
apps.explanation: Models can memorise and leak training data. Privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy are needed to prevent data extraction.

apps.name: An AI system automatically denies loan applications. The denial process is fully automated with no option for applicants to discuss the decision or have it reviewed by a person.
apps.explanation: High-stakes decisions affecting people's livelihoods require a meaningful human in the loop who can review and override automated decisions.

challenges.explanation: The four pillars of responsible AI are distinct but interconnected. Transparency ensures decisions can be understood. Accountability ensures someone is responsible. Privacy protects user data. Human oversight ensures automated decisions can be reviewed and overridden by people.

blocks.title: Building Responsible AI Systems
blocks.body: Responsible AI is not a one-time certification — it is a continuous practice that must be embedded at every stage of the development lifecycle. The most important principle is to design for the worst case from the start.
bullets: Start with data governance — know where your data came from, who it represents, and what biases it contains
Design for the worst case — assume your model will make mistakes and build monitoring, rollbacks, and escalation paths
Audit continuously, not once — fairness and safety are properties that must be monitored over time as the world changes

data.body: A pre-deployment audit is not bureaucratic overhead — it is the last line of defence before a system impacts real people. The audit above checks five pillars of responsible AI. Failing even one check should be a blocking issue for deployment. In practice, organisations that deploy responsibly treat audit results as binding, not advisory.

blocks.title: Practice Exercise
blocks.instructions: A hiring algorithm made decisions on 6 candidates from two groups. Run the fairness audit below. Identify whether the algorithm treats both groups equally and which fairness metric reveals the bias.
blocks.starterCode:
# Hiring algorithm audit: does it treat Group A and Group B equally?

decisions = [
    {'name': 'Alice', 'group': 'A', 'qualified': True,  'hired': True },
    {'name': 'Bob',   'group': 'B', 'qualified': True,  'hired': False},
    {'name': 'Carol', 'group': 'A', 'qualified': False, 'hired': False},
    {'name': 'Dan',   'group': 'B', 'qualified': True,  'hired': False},
    {'name': 'Eve',   'group': 'A', 'qualified': True,  'hired': True },
    {'name': 'Frank', 'group': 'B', 'qualified': False, 'hired': False},
]

for group in ['A', 'B']:
    g       = [d for d in decisions if d['group'] == group]
    qual    = [d for d in g if d['qualified']]
    hired   = [d for d in g if d['hired']]
    tpr     = len([d for d in qual if d['hired']]) / len(qual) if qual else 0
    overall = len(hired) / len(g)

    print(f"Group {group}:")
    print(f"  Total candidates      : {len(g)}")
    print(f"  Qualified candidates  : {len(qual)}")
    print(f"  Hired                 : {len(hired)}")
    print(f"  Overall hire rate     : {overall:.0%}")
    print(f"  True Positive Rate    : {tpr:.0%}  (qualified who got hired)")
    print()

print("⚠  Group B has 2 qualified candidates but 0 were hired.")
print("   True Positive Rate: Group A = 100%, Group B = 0%")
print("   This is a textbook example of algorithmic bias.")
print()
print("Ethical AI requires equal True Positive Rates across groups.")
blocks.solution:
decisions=[{'g':'A','q':True,'h':True},{'g':'B','q':True,'h':False},{'g':'A','q':False,'h':False},{'g':'B','q':True,'h':False},{'g':'A','q':True,'h':True},{'g':'B','q':False,'h':False}]
for grp in['A','B']:
    g=[d for d in decisions if d['g']==grp];q=[d for d in g if d['q']]
    tpr=len([d for d in q if d['h']])/len(q) if q else 0
    print(f"Group {grp} TPR: {tpr:.0%}")
blocks.hint: True Positive Rate (TPR) = qualified candidates who were actually hired. If Group A TPR = 100% and Group B TPR = 0%, the algorithm is biased regardless of overall accuracy.

keyTakeaways.text: Algorithmic bias emerges when training data encodes historical human biases
Removing protected attributes does not remove bias — proxy variables remain
Disparate impact ratio below 0.8 indicates potential discriminatory outcomes
Language models have no concept of truth — they generate probable, not true, continuations
AI hallucinations are confident fabrications — always verify high-stakes factual claims
Deepfakes are synthetic media indistinguishable from real — detection is an arms race
Responsible AI requires transparency, accountability, privacy, and human oversight
Fairness, safety, and ethics are design requirements, not afterthought patches

whatYouLearned: What algorithmic bias is, where it comes from, and why removing protected attributes doesn't fix it
How to measure disparate impact using the 80% rule
What AI hallucinations are and why language models produce them
What deepfakes are and how detection approaches work
The four pillars of responsible AI: transparency, accountability, privacy, human oversight
How to conduct a basic AI deployment audit
Why AI ethics is not optional at the scale AI is being deployed
